subject: Psychiatry
q: A 17-year-old competitive gymnast presents with amenorrhoea for 6 months, a tibial stress fracture, and a BMI of 17 kg/m2 while deliberately restricting food intake to stay lean. Which triad best explains her presentation?
why: Cushing syndrome causes weight gain and hypertension, not this lean athletic picture.
PCOS causes hyperandrogenic oligomenorrhoea, usually with higher BMI, not stress fractures from low BMD.
Correct - chronic energy deficit suppresses the HPG axis, causing amenorrhoea and low bone density.
Turner syndrome is a congenital karyotype disorder with primary amenorrhoea, not an acquired athletic condition.
exp: Female athlete triad (now often framed as Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport, RED-S) links low energy availability to hypothalamic amenorrhoea and low bone mineral density - a stress fracture in a young athlete with amenorrhoea should always prompt screening for disordered eating.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
q: A 30-year-old man has had continuous psychotic symptoms for 8 months. For 5 of those months he also met criteria for a major depressive episode; for the remaining 3 months he had persecutory delusions and hallucinations with no mood symptoms at all. Which diagnosis fits best?
why: Brief psychotic disorder lasts under 1 month, far shorter than this 8-month course.
In psychotic depression, psychosis occurs only during mood episodes, unlike this patient's 3 psychosis-only months.
Schizophreniform disorder applies when total illness duration is 1-6 months; this has run 8 months.
Correct - psychosis for at least 2 weeks without a mood episode plus substantial mood episodes fits schizoaffective disorder.
exp: The diagnostic key to schizoaffective disorder is a two-week or longer window of psychotic symptoms with no concurrent mood episode - this is what separates it from a mood disorder with psychotic features, where psychosis never occurs independent of mood symptoms.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 35-year-old woman reports excessive, difficult-to-control worry about her job, finances, and family's health for the past 8 months, along with muscle tension, restlessness, and poor sleep, but no discrete panic attacks. Most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct - excessive, hard-to-control worry across domains for six or more months with somatic symptoms defines GAD.
Panic disorder features discrete, recurrent panic attacks, which are absent here.
Adjustment disorder requires a clear identifiable stressor within the preceding 3 months, not stated here.
Illness anxiety disorder centres on preoccupation with having a serious illness, not general life worries.
exp: GAD is defined by chronic (six months or more), free-floating worry across multiple life domains plus at least three of: restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance - distinguishing it from the episodic, discrete attacks of panic disorder.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 45-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is brought to the emergency department confused, with nystagmus and a broad-based gait, after paramedics gave him IV dextrose for field hypoglycemia. His confusion has since worsened. What management error most likely precipitated this?
opts: Naloxone should have been given first
Thiamine should have been given before or with the dextrose to prevent precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy
Flumazenil should have been given first
Dextrose was contraindicated and should not have been given at all
why: There is no opioid intoxication picture here; naloxone is not indicated.
Correct - thiamine should be given before or with glucose to prevent precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy.
There is no benzodiazepine overdose picture; flumazenil can precipitate seizures in dependent patients.
Dextrose is still needed for hypoglycemia; the fix is adding thiamine, not withholding glucose.
exp: In any suspected chronically malnourished or alcohol-dependent patient, thiamine should be given before or together with intravenous glucose - glucose-driven carbohydrate metabolism depletes residual thiamine and can precipitate acute Wernicke's encephalopathy (confusion, nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia, broad-based ataxia).

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 28-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has had 5 distinct mood episodes (a mix of manic and depressive) over the past 12 months, each separated by remission or a switch in polarity. This pattern is termed:
why: The mixed features specifier describes one episode with simultaneous manic and depressive symptoms, not this pattern.
Cyclothymia is a 2-year pattern of sub-threshold symptoms never meeting full episode criteria.
Correct - rapid cycling is defined as four or more mood episodes within 12 months.
Ultradian cycling refers to mood switches within a single day, a much faster and rarer pattern.
exp: Rapid cycling (four or more episodes per year) is a course specifier, not a distinct diagnosis, and predicts poorer response to lithium monotherapy - anticonvulsant mood stabilizers such as valproate are often preferred.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 32-year-old man is found in another city, unable to recall his identity or how he got there. He has lived under an assumed name for 2 weeks, otherwise functioning normally, after a major financial loss and marital conflict. No organic cause is found. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Dissociative amnesia alone lacks the purposeful travel and new-identity assumption seen here
Depersonalization-derealization involves detachment/unreality without memory loss or travel
Correct — sudden travel, new identity, and amnesia after severe stress define dissociative fugue
Malingering is deliberate feigning for secondary gain, not indicated by this genuine functional presentation
exp: Dissociative fugue involves sudden, unexplained travel with inability to recall one's past and assumption of a new identity, typically triggered by severe psychosocial stress.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 24-year-old man is evaluated after repeatedly watching an unsuspecting neighbor undress through her window over 8 months, deriving sexual arousal from this, with significant distress and having acted on the urges multiple times. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Exhibitionistic disorder involves exposing one's own genitals, not observing others
Frotteuristic disorder involves touching/rubbing against a non-consenting person
Fetishistic disorder involves arousal from objects or specific body parts, not voyeuristic observation
Correct — recurrent arousal from observing an unsuspecting person, acted on with distress, defines voyeuristic disorder
exp: Voyeuristic disorder requires recurrent, intense arousal from observing an unsuspecting person naked/disrobing for at least 6 months, with acting on the urges or resulting distress.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 40-year-old woman reports persistently low mood, poor appetite, low energy, and low self-esteem for the past 2 years, never symptom-free for more than 2 months at a stretch, with no manic/hypomanic history, and symptoms not always meeting full major-depressive-episode severity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — depressed mood most days for at least 2 years with no symptom-free period over 2 months defines persistent depressive disorder
Recurrent MDD involves discrete episodes with inter-episode recovery, unlike this continuous course
Cyclothymia involves alternating subthreshold depressive and hypomanic symptoms, not purely depressive ones
Adjustment disorder is time-limited to within 3 months of a stressor, not a chronic 2-year course
exp: Persistent depressive disorder requires depressed mood most of the day, more days than not, for at least 2 years, with no symptom-free period exceeding 2 months.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department unconscious, with a respiratory rate of 6/min and pinpoint pupils; track marks are noted on his forearms. What is the immediate treatment of choice?
why: Flumazenil is for benzodiazepine overdose and risks precipitating seizures here
Correct — naloxone rapidly reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression
N-acetylcysteine is the paracetamol overdose antidote
Physostigmine is for anticholinergic toxicity
exp: The classic opioid overdose triad (coma, respiratory depression, miosis) with track marks is diagnostic of opioid toxicity; naloxone reverses it, though repeat dosing may be needed.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
q: A 22-year-old student develops persecutory delusions, auditory hallucinations, and disorganized speech for the past 3 months with significant functional decline, no mood episode, and symptoms not yet 6 months in duration. What is the most likely diagnosis at this point?
why: Brief psychotic disorder lasts only 1 day to 1 month, far shorter than this 3-month course
Schizophrenia needs at least 6 months of continuous disturbance, not yet met
Correct — Criterion-A symptoms for 1 to under 6 months define schizophreniform disorder
Schizoaffective disorder needs a concurrent major mood episode overlapping the psychosis, absent here
exp: Schizophreniform disorder is diagnosed when psychotic symptoms persist at least 1 month but under 6 months; beyond 6 months the diagnosis becomes schizophrenia.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 24-year-old unmarried man from a rural background presents with fatigue, weakness, and anxiety, which he attributes to loss of semen through nocturnal emissions and masturbation, believing this depletes his vital energy. There is no evidence of any underlying medical or psychotic illness. This culture-bound presentation, common in the Indian subcontinent, is termed:
why: Koro is the culture-bound fear of genital retraction/shrinkage, a different presentation
Focuses on perceived defects in physical appearance, not semen loss
Correct
Not specific to this culturally framed belief about semen loss
exp: Dhat syndrome is a culture-bound syndrome described predominantly in South Asia, characterized by vague somatic complaints (fatigue, weakness, anxiety) attributed by the patient to loss of semen, often with excessive health anxiety about sexual function.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 45-year-old man on long-term lithium therapy for bipolar disorder is started on a thiazide diuretic for newly diagnosed hypertension. Two weeks later, he develops coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, and vomiting. The most likely explanation is:
opts: Lithium toxicity due to thiazide-induced reduced renal lithium clearance
Serotonin syndrome from a drug interaction
Hyponatremia from thiazide alone, unrelated to lithium levels
why: Correct
Serotonin syndrome requires a serotonergic agent, not a thiazide
The clinical picture (coarse tremor, ataxia) is classic for lithium toxicity, not isolated hyponatremia
NMS is linked to antipsychotics, with rigidity and hyperthermia as core features, not this picture
exp: Thiazide diuretics cause volume contraction and compensatory increased proximal tubular sodium (and secondarily lithium) reabsorption, raising serum lithium levels and precipitating toxicity - lithium levels must be monitored whenever thiazides are co-prescribed.

subject: Psychiatry
q: An 8-year-old boy has restricted his diet to only four specific foods since early childhood because of sensitivity to their texture and smell, resulting in significant weight loss and nutritional deficiency. He shows no fear of gaining weight and no disturbance in how he perceives his body shape. This presentation is most consistent with:
why: Requires body image disturbance/fear of weight gain, absent here
Correct
Involves eating non-nutritive substances, not food avoidance
Involves repeated regurgitation and re-chewing of food, not restrictive eating
exp: ARFID (DSM-5) involves avoidance or restriction of food intake leading to nutritional deficiency or weight loss, driven by sensory sensitivity, lack of interest in eating, or fear of aversive consequences - crucially without the body-image disturbance or fear of weight gain that defines anorexia nervosa.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 38-year-old man with chronic heavy alcohol use has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure 18 hours after his last drink, before any hallucinations or significant autonomic hyperactivity have appeared. This timing is most consistent with:
why: Occurs later, with prominent autonomic/confusional features not yet present here
Presents with the classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia from thiamine deficiency, not this timing picture
Presents with hallucinations without the confusion of DTs, not the best fit for this timing
Correct
exp: Alcohol withdrawal seizures classically occur early, within 6-48 hours (peaking around 12-30 hours) after the last drink, preceding delirium tremens, which typically peaks at 48-96 hours with prominent autonomic instability, confusion, and hallucinations.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 30-year-old man repeatedly presents to different hospitals with dramatic, fabricated illness histories, undergoing multiple invasive investigations and even surgeries, with no identifiable external incentive such as financial compensation, disability benefits, or avoiding legal/work responsibilities - his apparent motivation is simply to assume the sick role. This presentation is most consistent with:
why: Requires an identifiable external incentive, absent here
Symptoms are genuinely experienced, not intentionally fabricated
Correct
Characterized by excessive worry about having an illness, not deliberate fabrication
exp: Factitious disorder involves intentional fabrication or induction of symptoms in the absence of external secondary gain, motivated by an internal need to assume the sick role - distinguishing it from malingering (external gain) and somatic symptom/illness anxiety disorders (symptoms/worry not intentionally produced).

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 30-year-old man presents with a persistent, 8-month preoccupation that he has a serious undiagnosed illness, despite having minimal or no actual somatic symptoms; he repeatedly checks his body for signs of disease and seeks reassurance from multiple doctors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Wrong - requires significant, distressing somatic symptoms, which are minimal or absent here
Correct - health anxiety with minimal somatic symptoms fits illness anxiety disorder
Wrong - conversion disorder involves neurological-type symptoms, not health preoccupation
Wrong - factitious disorder involves deliberate symptom fabrication for the sick role, not genuine anxiety
exp: Illness anxiety disorder (formerly hypochondriasis) is characterized by high health-related anxiety and preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness, with minimal or absent somatic symptoms - distinguishing it from somatic symptom disorder, where prominent, distressing physical symptoms dominate.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 34-year-old woman on fluoxetine for major depressive disorder for the past 2 months reports new difficulty achieving orgasm and reduced libido that are distressing and affecting her relationship, even though her mood has clearly improved. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: Onset of a primary sexual desire disorder unrelated to medication
why: Wrong - mood has improved, arguing against worsening depression as the cause
Wrong - the temporal link to starting fluoxetine points to a medication effect, not a primary disorder
Correct - new sexual dysfunction coinciding with SSRI initiation and improved mood is classic for medication-induced dysfunction
Wrong - no history suggests primary relationship conflict as the driver
exp: SSRIs commonly cause sexual side effects - reduced libido, delayed orgasm, or anorgasmia - via increased serotonergic tone; management options include dose reduction, switching to an agent with a lower sexual side-effect profile (bupropion, mirtazapine), or adding a PDE5 inhibitor.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 40-year-old woman with severe major depressive disorder with psychotic features has refused food and water for 3 days, is severely dehydrated, and expresses active suicidal intent with a specific plan. Given the urgency, which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Start an SSRI and reassess in 4-6 weeks
why: Wrong - SSRIs take weeks to act, too slow for this life-threatening presentation
Wrong - psychotherapy alone is inappropriate for acute, severe, psychotic, medically compromised depression
Wrong - a benzodiazepine alone does not treat the underlying depressive/psychotic illness
Correct - ECT provides the rapid response this emergency requires
exp: ECT is indicated as a rapid, first-line treatment when a fast antidepressant response is critical - high imminent suicide risk, psychotic depression, catatonia, or medical compromise from refusal of food and fluids - situations where waiting weeks for pharmacotherapy to work is unsafe.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A known intravenous drug user with track marks on both forearms is brought to casualty 14 hours after his last dose, restless and complaining of severe muscle aches, with lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, piloerection, yawning, dilated pupils, and diarrhoea, but he remains fully oriented with normal vital signs otherwise. What is the most likely clinical state?
why: Wrong - opioid intoxication causes pinpoint pupils, sedation, and respiratory depression, the opposite picture
Correct - the classic opioid withdrawal syndrome and its timeline
Wrong - delirium tremens is an alcohol withdrawal phenomenon with confusion and hallucinations, not this clear-sensorium picture with dilated pupils
Wrong - anticholinergic toxicity causes dry mucosa and dilated pupils but also delirium/hyperthermia and urinary retention, not lacrimation/rhinorrhoea/diarrhoea
exp: Opioid withdrawal classically begins 6-12 hours after the last dose for short-acting opioids like heroin (24-48 hours for methadone), producing lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, piloerection, yawning, dilated pupils (the opposite of intoxication's pinpoint pupils), muscle aches, and diarrhoea. It is intensely distressing but not life-threatening, unlike alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal. Management is supportive plus opioid agonist substitution (buprenorphine/methadone) or clonidine for autonomic symptoms.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
q: A 28-year-old man on haloperidol for schizophrenia develops high-grade fever, generalized muscle rigidity, altered sensorium, and autonomic instability (tachycardia, labile blood pressure) over 2 days; serum creatine kinase is markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?
opts: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; stop the antipsychotic, give supportive care with dantrolene or bromocriptine if needed
Malignant catatonia; continue the antipsychotic and add a benzodiazepine
why: Wrong - serotonin syndrome is linked to serotonergic drugs and features hyperreflexia/clonus, not this antipsychotic-linked rigidity picture
Correct - this is the classic NMS presentation and its correct emergency management
Wrong - acute dystonia is a focal, brief muscle spasm, not this systemic syndrome
Wrong - continuing the antipsychotic in a suspected NMS-spectrum illness is dangerous; the offending drug must be stopped
exp: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome presents with fever, lead-pipe rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability, typically after starting or increasing a high-potency antipsychotic, with markedly elevated CK from muscle breakdown; management is immediate drug discontinuation plus supportive care, reserving dantrolene or bromocriptine for severe or refractory cases.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
q: A 35-year-old man believes his wife has been replaced by an identical impostor, and this belief persists despite reassurance and evidence to the contrary from family members. Which delusional misidentification syndrome does this represent?
why: Correct — impostor-replacement delusion
Fregoli syndrome is the opposite belief — that different people are actually a single person in disguise
Cotard syndrome is the nihilistic delusion of being dead or not existing
De Clerambault syndrome is the delusional belief that another person, often of higher status, is in love with the patient
exp: Capgras syndrome is the delusional belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an identical-looking impostor; it is classically associated with schizophrenia but can also occur with dementia or focal brain lesions affecting face-recognition and familiarity circuits.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 28-year-old software engineer reports recurrent, unexpected episodes of palpitations, sweating, chest tightness and a fear of dying, each lasting about 10 minutes, followed by persistent worry about having another episode. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — matches discrete unexpected attacks plus anticipatory anxiety
GAD involves persistent, diffuse worry across domains without the discrete attack pattern described
Social anxiety disorder is situational, tied to social/performance settings, not unexpected
Somatic symptom disorder involves chronic preoccupation with physical symptoms without this episodic autonomic pattern
exp: Panic disorder is defined by DSM-5 as recurrent, unexpected panic attacks followed by at least a month of persistent worry about further attacks or their consequences (anticipatory anxiety), distinguishing it from GAD's chronic, diffuse worry without discrete attacks.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 30-year-old man is arrested for repeatedly touching and rubbing against unsuspecting persons in crowded public transport for sexual gratification, a pattern present for over 6 months. Which paraphilic disorder does this describe?
why: Voyeurism involves secretly observing an unsuspecting person who is naked or engaged in sexual activity, not physical contact
Exhibitionism involves exposing one's genitals to an unsuspecting person
Correct — matches the touching/rubbing behaviour in crowded settings
Sexual sadism involves arousal from inflicting physical or psychological suffering
exp: Frotteuristic disorder involves recurrent, intense sexual arousal from touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person, typically in crowded settings that allow escape, present for at least 6 months and either acted upon or causing significant distress/impairment.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 45-year-old man with chronic heavy alcohol use is admitted for elective surgery. On the second day post-admission, he develops coarse tremors, agitation, visual hallucinations, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, fever) and disorientation. What is the most likely diagnosis, and its typical onset window after the last drink?
opts: Simple/uncomplicated alcohol withdrawal, typically within 6-12 hours
Delirium tremens, typically 48-96 hours after the last drink
why: Alcoholic hallucinosis occurs earlier with a clear sensorium (no disorientation), unlike this patient
Simple withdrawal presents earlier with milder autonomic symptoms and no clouding of consciousness
Correct — matches both the clinical picture (disorientation plus autonomic storm) and the typical timing
Wernicke's presents with the ataxia-ophthalmoplegia-confusion triad from thiamine deficiency, not this picture
exp: Delirium tremens is a life-threatening alcohol withdrawal emergency characterized by coarse tremor, marked autonomic hyperactivity, hallucinations, agitation, and a clouded, disoriented sensorium, classically emerging 48-96 hours after the last drink and requiring aggressive benzodiazepine treatment. Exact hour cut-offs vary slightly by textbook.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 19-year-old woman with a 2-year history of self-induced vomiting after most meals is noted to have calluses on the dorsum of her hand, along with enamel erosion on the lingual (inner) surface of her upper front teeth. What is this hand finding called?
why: Chvostek's sign is facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve, a sign of hypocalcemia
Nikolsky's sign is skin sloughing with lateral pressure, seen in pemphigus/SSSS
Trousseau's sign is carpal spasm with BP cuff inflation, also a hypocalcemia sign
Correct — the purging-related hand sign
exp: Russell's sign refers to calluses or abrasions over the knuckles/dorsum of the hand from repeated friction against the teeth during self-induced vomiting; together with dental enamel erosion and parotid gland enlargement, it is a classic physical clue to chronic purging behaviour in bulimia nervosa.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
q: A 22-year-old college student presents with mutism, waxy flexibility, abnormal posturing and negativism for the past 3 days, following an episode of acute psychosis. Which clinical syndrome best describes this presentation, and which class of drug is first-line treatment?
opts: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; treated with dantrolene
Catatonia; treated with benzodiazepines (e.g., a lorazepam challenge)
Locked-in syndrome; treated with supportive care only
why: NMS additionally features fever, muscle rigidity and autonomic instability, usually following antipsychotic exposure — not the picture described, and dantrolene is not first-line for catatonia
Correct — matches the psychomotor features and standard first-line treatment
Malignant hyperthermia is an anaesthetic-triggered hypermetabolic crisis, unrelated to this presentation
Locked-in syndrome is due to a pontine lesion with preserved consciousness, not a psychiatric syndrome
exp: Catatonia is a psychomotor syndrome that can complicate psychotic, mood, or medical disorders; benzodiazepines (classically a lorazepam challenge, both diagnostic and therapeutic) are first-line treatment, with ECT reserved for refractory or malignant catatonia.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 28-year-old heterosexual man reports recurrent, intense sexual arousal for over 6 months from handling and smelling women's shoes, unrelated to cross-dressing, causing him marked distress and interpersonal difficulty. Which paraphilic disorder is most likely?
why: Correct - recurrent arousal from a nonliving object over 6 months causing distress is fetishistic disorder
Transvestic disorder requires arousal from the act of cross-dressing itself, not the object alone
Voyeurism is arousal from observing an unsuspecting person naked or engaged in sexual activity
Frotteurism is touching or rubbing against a non-consenting person
exp: Fetishistic disorder (DSM-5) is recurrent, intense sexual arousal from nonliving objects (e.g. footwear, undergarments) or specific non-genital body parts, present over 6 months and causing distress or impairment; it excludes items used solely for cross-dressing.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 30-year-old road traffic accident survivor develops intrusive flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance of driving, hypervigilance, and emotional numbing persisting for 2 months since the event. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Acute stress disorder can only be diagnosed within the first month post-trauma
Correct - symptoms persisting beyond 1 month with re-experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal confirm PTSD
Adjustment disorder lacks the specific re-experiencing/avoidance/hyperarousal cluster and need not follow a traumatic stressor
GAD is pervasive free-floating worry unrelated to a specific trauma, without flashbacks
exp: PTSD requires exposure to a traumatic event followed by re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition/mood, and hyperarousal, persisting beyond 1 month; symptoms lasting under a month are classified as acute stress disorder instead.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 16-year-old assigned male at birth reports persistent, marked incongruence between experienced gender and assigned sex for over 2 years, with significant distress and a desire to be treated as female. Which DSM-5 diagnosis fits best?
why: Correct - marked incongruence with distress for over 6 months defines gender dysphoria
Transvestic disorder involves cross-dressing for sexual arousal, not gender identity incongruence
BDD involves preoccupation with a perceived appearance defect, not gender identity
Dissociative identity disorder involves distinct personality states, unrelated to gender identity
exp: DSM-5 gender dysphoria requires marked incongruence between experienced/expressed gender and assigned gender for at least 6 months, with clinically significant distress or impairment.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 16-year-old girl with a 6-month history of severe caloric restriction and a BMI of 15 kg/m2 presents with bradycardia, hypotension, lanugo hair over the back, and secondary amenorrhea. Which mechanism best explains the amenorrhea?
opts: Hypothalamic suppression of GnRH pulsatility due to low body weight/energy deficit
why: Correct - functional hypothalamic amenorrhea from energy deficit
Primary ovarian failure would show a hypergonadotropic pattern (high FSH/LH), not this picture
Hyperprolactinemia is not a typical feature of anorexia-related amenorrhea
PCOS is associated with obesity/hyperandrogenism, the opposite of a wasting picture
exp: Severe caloric restriction and low body fat in anorexia nervosa suppress hypothalamic GnRH pulsatile secretion, leading to low LH/FSH and estrogen - reversible with weight restoration.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 35-year-old man is brought for evaluation after repeatedly exposing his genitals to unsuspecting strangers over the past 8 months, experiencing intense arousal from the act and significant distress about the behavior. Which paraphilic disorder does this describe?
why: Voyeuristic disorder involves observing an unsuspecting person, not exposing oneself
Correct - recurrent arousal from exposing genitals to unsuspecting persons defines exhibitionistic disorder
Fetishistic disorder involves arousal from nonliving objects or specific non-genital body parts
Frotteuristic disorder involves touching/rubbing against a non-consenting person
exp: Exhibitionistic disorder (DSM-5) involves recurrent, intense sexual arousal from exposing one's genitals to an unsuspecting person, occurring over at least 6 months, causing distress or impairment.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 17-year-old girl reports intense fear of gaining weight, restrictive eating, and significant unintentional weight loss over 4 months, but her current BMI remains within the normal range for age. Which DSM-5 diagnosis best fits?
why: Classic anorexia nervosa requires a significantly low body weight, not present here
Correct - all AN criteria met except weight remains in the normal range
Bulimia nervosa involves binge-purge cycles, not described here
ARFID lacks the weight/body-image concerns central to this case
exp: Atypical anorexia nervosa applies when all criteria for anorexia nervosa are met except that weight remains within or above the normal range despite significant loss - it is increasingly recognized and carries comparable medical risk.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 35-year-old man reports sudden-onset erectile dysfunction with his partner over the past two months, but says he still wakes with firm morning erections and can achieve erections during masturbation. What does this pattern suggest about the aetiology?
opts: Organic erectile dysfunction, likely neurogenic (e.g. diabetic autonomic neuropathy)
why: Vascular ED typically impairs erections in all settings, including sleep, with gradual onset
Correct
Neurogenic ED likewise impairs nocturnal erections and has a gradual course
Hypogonadism reduces libido/erections globally, not just with a partner
exp: Preserved nocturnal/morning and masturbatory erections with situational sudden-onset failure points to a psychogenic cause, since the reflex/nocturnal erectile pathway, which doesn't require psychological arousal, remains intact. Nocturnal penile tumescence testing formalises this distinction when history is unclear.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 26-year-old man reports that in nearly all sexual encounters over the past 8 months, ejaculation occurs within about 30 seconds of vaginal penetration, well before he wishes, causing him significant distress and avoidance of intimacy. Which is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?
why: Sildenafil (a PDE5 inhibitor) treats erectile dysfunction, not ejaculatory control, and is not first-line here
Topical anaesthetic creams are a second-line/adjunct option that reduces penile sensitivity, but SSRIs remain first-line pharmacotherapy
Correct — dapoxetine's on-demand serotonergic action delays ejaculation and is a recognised first-line drug therapy
Testosterone addresses hypogonadism/libido, not the serotonergic ejaculatory reflex
exp: Lifelong or acquired premature ejaculation with an intravaginal ejaculatory latency time under about 1 minute causing distress meets DSM-5 criteria; on-demand dapoxetine, a short-acting SSRI dosed 1-3 hours before intercourse, is first-line pharmacotherapy by delaying ejaculation via serotonergic action, used alongside behavioural techniques like the stop-start or squeeze method.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 28-year-old woman reports recurrent weekly episodes of eating unusually large amounts of food with loss of control, followed by guilt, but no compensatory vomiting, laxative use, fasting, or excessive exercise. What is the most likely DSM-5 diagnosis?
why: Bulimia nervosa requires recurrent compensatory behaviors, explicitly absent here
Correct — binge eating without compensatory behavior defines BED
Anorexia binge-purge subtype requires significantly low body weight, not described
Night eating syndrome is an evening-hyperphagia/nocturnal-awakening pattern, not discrete binge episodes
exp: Binge eating disorder (DSM-5) is defined by recurrent binge eating (at least once weekly for 3 months) with marked distress, WITHOUT the regular compensatory behaviors that define bulimia nervosa — this absence of purging/compensation is the key discriminator, and patients are often overweight/obese.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 28-year-old man spends several hours daily washing his hands because of intrusive fears of contamination. He finds the urge unwanted, tries unsuccessfully to resist it, and it is causing him significant occupational impairment. Which feature of his presentation most favours obsessive-compulsive disorder over a psychotic disorder?
opts: Fixed, unshakeable false belief without insight
Insight that the thoughts/behaviors are excessive and irrational (ego-dystonic)
why: Hallucinations are a psychotic feature, not core to OCD
A fixed false belief without insight describes a delusion, the opposite of typical OCD
Thought broadcasting is a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia
Correct - ego-dystonic insight is the defining OCD feature
exp: One of the most characteristic distinctions between OCD and psychotic disorders is insight: OCD obsessions and compulsions are usually ego-dystonic - recognised as excessive or irrational even though the patient cannot resist them - whereas delusions in psychotic disorders are typically held with full conviction and without insight. DSM-5 does allow an OCD insight specifier down to 'absent insight/delusional beliefs', so insight is characteristic rather than absolute, but it remains the most useful bedside discriminator.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 30-year-old woman describes recurrent episodes of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, and increased goal-directed activity lasting about 5 days without impairing her ability to work, alternating with episodes meeting full criteria for major depression; she has never been hospitalised or had psychotic features. This presentation is most consistent with:
opts: Major depressive disorder with mixed features
why: Bipolar I requires at least one full manic episode, which is absent here
Cyclothymic disorder involves symptoms not meeting full episode criteria for at least 2 years, unlike her full major depressive episodes
Correct — hypomania plus major depression defines bipolar II
This patient has distinct episodes, not a single mixed episode of major depression
exp: Bipolar II disorder is defined by at least one hypomanic episode (minimum 4 days, elevated mood/energy without marked functional impairment, hospitalisation, or psychotic features) plus at least one major depressive episode; never meeting full manic-episode severity distinguishes it from bipolar I.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 19-year-old develops sudden bilateral leg weakness after witnessing an acute family conflict; examination shows normal reflexes and tone, MRI of the spine and brain is normal, and she appears strikingly calm and unconcerned about her paralysis (a presentation consistent with conversion disorder). This characteristic lack of concern is termed:
why: Alexithymia is difficulty identifying or describing one's own emotions, not a lack of concern about a physical symptom
Anosognosia is organic unawareness of a deficit, not a psychologically mediated lack of concern
Correct — la belle indifference is the classically described inappropriate calm seen in conversion disorder
Secondary gain refers to external benefits obtained from being unwell, not the patient's affect toward the symptom
exp: Conversion disorder presents with a neurological symptom inconsistent with recognised neuroanatomical pathways, precipitated or worsened by psychological stress. La belle indifference — an inappropriately calm attitude toward an ostensibly disabling symptom — is a classically described associated feature, though it is not a DSM-5-TR diagnostic criterion; the actual diagnostic requirement is demonstrable clinical inconsistency (e.g. Hoover's sign, give-way weakness) with normal reflexes and tone.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 24-year-old man is brought by family for 6 days of decreased need for sleep (3 hours/night, feels rested), rapid pressured speech, grandiose business plans he has already invested his savings into, and irritability when questioned. There is no psychosis. Which diagnosis best fits?
why: Cyclothymia is chronic fluctuating subsyndromal mood over 2 years, not this acute severe presentation
Correct, DSM-5 manic episode: at least 1 week of elevated/irritable mood plus at least 3 symptoms causing marked impairment such as reckless investment
Hypomania has similar symptoms but only 4+ days duration and no marked functional impairment - here there is impairment
No psychotic features described, so schizoaffective is not supported
exp: DSM-5 distinguishes mania from hypomania primarily by duration (7+ days vs 4+ days) and severity (marked impairment/hospitalization/psychosis vs no marked impairment). Reckless spending/investment causing functional harm tips this into a manic, not hypomanic, episode - a common NEET PG discriminator.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 45-year-old woman describes 3 weeks of pervasive loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, mood that is distinctly worse in the mornings and lifts somewhat by evening, a 5 kg weight loss without dieting, early morning awakening 2 hours before her usual time, and marked psychomotor slowing noted by her family. Which specifier best describes this depressive episode?
why: Atypical depression features mood reactivity, hypersomnia, increased appetite/weight gain, and leaden paralysis - opposite of this picture
Peripartum onset applies only during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum
Catatonic features require specific motor abnormalities (stupor, catalepsy, mutism), not described
Correct, anhedonia, diurnal mood variation, early morning awakening, weight loss, psychomotor disturbance
exp: Melancholic features (worse mornings, early morning awakening, marked anhedonia, significant weight loss, psychomotor retardation) predict a strong biological/somatic depression and better response to antidepressants/ECT - distinct from atypical depression, which often responds preferentially to MAOIs.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
q: A 24-year-old man reports that his private thoughts are being transmitted so that people around him can directly hear them, alongside auditory hallucinations discussing his actions. Which Schneiderian first-rank symptom is described first?
why: Wrong — insertion is thoughts being placed into one's mind by an outside agency, not transmitted outward.
Correct — broadcasting is the belief that one's own thoughts are transmitted so others can perceive them.
Wrong — withdrawal is thoughts being removed/taken away, not broadcast outward.
Wrong — delusional perception is a normal percept with an abnormal, delusional significance attached, unrelated to thought content transmission.
exp: Schneider's first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia include thought broadcasting (own thoughts transmitted so others can perceive them), thought insertion (thoughts placed into the mind by an external agency), thought withdrawal (thoughts removed by an outside force), running commentary/third-person auditory hallucinations, somatic passivity, and delusional perception. DSM-5 no longer gives them special diagnostic weight, but they remain high-yield descriptive psychopathology.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 30-year-old woman has recurrent, unexplained multiple physical complaints (GI, sexual, pseudo-neurological, pain) over several years, with extensive negative work-ups, causing significant distress and repeated doctor visits. What is the diagnosis?
why: Wrong — illness anxiety disorder is preoccupation with having a disease, with few or no actual somatic symptoms.
Correct — multiple, longstanding physical complaints with distress and care-seeking despite negative work-up is classic somatic symptom disorder.
Wrong — conversion disorder presents as a specific neurological deficit incompatible with disease, not multiple vague complaints.
Wrong — factitious disorder involves conscious fabrication of symptoms for internal psychological gain, not genuine distress.
exp: DSM-5 somatic symptom disorder requires one or more distressing somatic symptoms plus excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to those symptoms, persisting beyond 6 months, regardless of whether a medical cause is found. Differs from illness anxiety disorder (preoccupation with illness, minimal symptoms), conversion disorder (specific neurological symptom incompatible with disease), and factitious disorder (intentional fabrication for the sick role).

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 17-year-old girl weighs 30% below expected body weight, has an intense fear of gaining weight, and denies the seriousness of her low weight despite severe emaciation. Which DSM-5 diagnostic criterion is illustrated by her denial?
opts: Disturbance in self-perceived body weight/shape, or lack of recognition of the seriousness of low body weight
why: Correct — denial of the seriousness of low weight is precisely DSM-5 criterion C (body image disturbance/lack of insight).
Wrong — binge eating episodes characterize bulimia nervosa or binge-eating disorder, not the restricting-type anorexia described here.
Wrong — purging is a compensatory behavior seen in bulimia or the binge-purge subtype of anorexia, not what is illustrated by her denial.
Wrong — amenorrhea was a DSM-IV criterion, removed in DSM-5, and is not what her denial of severity illustrates.
exp: DSM-5 anorexia nervosa criteria: restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight; intense fear of gaining weight or persistent behavior interfering with weight gain; a disturbance in the way body weight/shape is experienced, undue influence on self-evaluation, or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight. Amenorrhea was removed as a required criterion in DSM-5.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 24-year-old newly married woman presents with inability to consummate her marriage of 6 months. She describes severe pain and a sensation of the opening being too tight whenever penetration is attempted, and this now happens even during a gynaecological speculum examination. Pelvic examination shows normal external genitalia and no organic pathology, but the examination could not be completed because of involuntary tightening of the pelvic floor muscles. What is the most likely diagnosis and its first-line management?
opts: Dyspareunia due to endometriosis; laparoscopic excision
Hypoactive sexual desire disorder; testosterone therapy
Vaginismus; graded vaginal dilators combined with pelvic floor relaxation and cognitive behavioural/sex therapy
why: Endometriosis-related dyspareunia causes deep pain with intercourse and pelvic pathology on exam/imaging, not involuntary muscle spasm preventing entry
HSDD is a lack of desire, not painful involuntary spasm, and testosterone is not standard first-line therapy
MRKH presents as primary amenorrhoea with an absent/hypoplastic vagina and uterus on exam — here the external genitalia and exam findings are anatomically normal
Correct — vaginismus is a functional disorder treated with dilators/physiotherapy/CBT, not surgery
exp: Vaginismus is involuntary spasm of the pelvic floor/perivaginal muscles triggered by anticipated penetration, occurring despite normal anatomy — recurrent involuntary tightening on attempted examination, not a structural finding, is the giveaway. First-line management is a graded desensitisation programme with vaginal dilators, pelvic floor physiotherapy, and CBT/sex therapy; surgery has no role since the anatomy is normal.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A woman develops tearfulness, mood lability, and anxiety on day 3 after delivery, resolving spontaneously within 2 weeks without treatment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct - classic timing (day 3) and spontaneous resolution within 2 weeks fits postpartum blues
Postpartum depression persists beyond 2 weeks and requires intervention, unlike this self-limiting course
Postpartum psychosis presents with psychotic features such as delusions or hallucinations, not isolated tearfulness/lability
Adjustment disorder requires an identifiable psychosocial stressor and a different diagnostic time frame
exp: Postpartum blues typically peaks around day 3-5 after delivery and self-resolves within 2 weeks, needing only reassurance and support - distinguish by timing and self-limited course from postpartum depression (persists beyond 2 weeks, needs treatment) and postpartum psychosis (psychiatric emergency with delusions/hallucinations).

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 19-year-old woman with normal BMI reports recurrent binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting for the past six months, with dental enamel erosion and calluses on her knuckles. Which electrolyte/acid-base abnormality is most characteristic of her purging behavior?
exp: Repeated vomiting loses gastric HCl and volume, producing hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Russell's sign (knuckle calluses from self-induced vomiting) and dental erosion are classic bulimia nervosa exam clues, distinct from anorexia's refeeding-related hypophosphatemia.

subject: Psychiatry
topic: Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
q: A 24-year-old man develops delusions of persecution and disorganized speech for 3 weeks following a major stressful life event, with full return to his baseline level of functioning once the symptoms resolve completely within one month. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exp: Brief psychotic disorder is defined by psychotic symptoms lasting less than 1 month with eventual full return to premorbid functioning, often precipitated by a clear stressor. Schizophreniform disorder requires 1-6 months of symptoms, and schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of continuous signs — duration and stressor context are the key discriminators.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 16-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa (BMI 13.5 kg/m2) is admitted for nutritional rehabilitation after 8 months of severe caloric restriction. On day 3 of controlled refeeding, she develops acute confusion, generalized weakness, and a new cardiac arrhythmia. Which electrolyte disturbance is most likely responsible?
exp: Refeeding syndrome in severely malnourished patients (classically anorexia nervosa) results from a carbohydrate-driven insulin surge that shifts phosphate intracellularly; the resulting hypophosphatemia drives cardiac arrhythmia, respiratory failure, and rhabdomyolysis. Prevention is slow caloric reintroduction with pre-emptive phosphate monitoring/supplementation.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 27-year-old married man presents with marked, persistent delay in reaching ejaculation during penetrative intercourse for the past 10 months, causing significant distress to him and his partner; he reports normal, timely ejaculation during masturbation and no erectile difficulty.
why: Premature ejaculation is the opposite pattern — occurring too early, not delayed.
Correct — situational delay with normal masturbatory ejaculation is classic for delayed ejaculation disorder.
Erection is explicitly normal, ruling out erectile dysfunction.
Hypoactive sexual desire disorder concerns reduced desire/fantasy, not a delayed ejaculatory reflex.
exp: Delayed ejaculation disorder (DSM-5-TR) is diagnosed when ejaculation is markedly delayed or infrequent/absent during partnered sexual activity for 6 months or more, causing distress, in a patient who ejaculates normally with masturbation — pointing to a psychogenic or situational cause rather than an organic one; management combines sex therapy with review of any contributing SSRI use.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A woman develops abrupt onset of agitation, insomnia, delusions that her 10-day-old baby is being replaced by an impostor, and command auditory hallucinations telling her to harm the infant; symptoms began on day 8 postpartum.
opts: Reassure her that this is postpartum blues and will resolve within two weeks
Start an SSRI as outpatient and review in 2 weeks
Admit her (with the infant, if a mother-baby unit is available) for urgent psychiatric evaluation and treatment
Advise supportive counselling alone as symptoms are stress-related
why: Postpartum blues is mild, self-limiting low mood without psychosis, peaking day 3–5 — this is far beyond blues.
Outpatient SSRI start is unsafe given active psychotic symptoms and risk to the infant.
Correct — postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency needing urgent admission and antipsychotic treatment given the infanticide/suicide risk.
Counselling alone dangerously delays treatment of an acute psychosis with risk to the infant.
exp: Postpartum psychosis typically presents within the first 2–4 weeks postpartum with abrupt-onset delusions, hallucinations (often involving the infant) and disorganised behaviour, and carries a real risk of infanticide or suicide — it is a psychiatric emergency needing urgent admission, unlike self-limiting postpartum blues.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 2-year-old from a rural household is brought with pallor and is repeatedly observed eating mud/soil from the courtyard for the past 4 months; investigations reveal microcytic hypochromic anemia.
why: ARFID is lack of interest in food or sensory-based avoidance, not ingestion of non-food items.
Rumination disorder is repeated regurgitation and re-chewing of already-swallowed food.
Atypical anorexia nervosa requires anorexia's cognitive/behavioural criteria with normal BMI — not applicable here.
Correct — persistent eating of a non-nutritive substance for a month or more, inappropriate to developmental age, defines pica.
exp: Pica is the persistent eating of non-nutritive, non-food substances for a month or more, common in young children and linked to iron-deficiency states in India — the relationship runs both ways, since iron deficiency can drive geophagia and soil ingestion can itself worsen anemia via GI parasitism, so iron studies and deworming should be checked alongside behavioural management.

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 32-year-old man has progressively increased his time on online betting/rummy apps over the past year, lying to family about losses, repeatedly attempting unsuccessfully to cut down, and borrowing money to continue playing despite mounting debt and job neglect.
why: OCD compulsions are typically ego-dystonic and anxiety-reducing, not reward-seeking like gambling.
A manic episode would also show elevated/irritable mood, reduced sleep need and grandiosity over days, not described here.
Correct — escalating involvement, failed attempts to cut back, chasing losses and lying to conceal it are the defining features of gambling disorder.
Adjustment disorder requires a clear stressor with a time-limited reaction, not this sustained pattern.
exp: Gambling disorder is DSM-5's only non-substance behavioural addiction, sharing the same core features as substance addiction — escalating involvement, failed attempts to cut down, preoccupation, chasing losses and concealment — and is an increasingly common India-specific presentation with online real-money gaming apps; treatment follows an addiction model (CBT, motivational interviewing, self-exclusion tools).

subject: Psychiatry
q: A 19-year-old college student spends over 3 hours daily checking her nose in the mirror, repeatedly seeking reassurance that it is 'too big and crooked,' and has dropped out of college due to distress, though examination shows an entirely normal, proportionate nose.
why: Somatic symptom disorder centres on distressing bodily symptoms, not appearance preoccupation.
Correct — preoccupation with a minimal or absent physical defect, with repetitive checking/reassurance-seeking and major functional impairment, defines body dysmorphic disorder.
Illness anxiety disorder is fear of serious illness with minimal somatic symptoms, not an appearance complaint.
Delusional disorder requires a fixed conviction with no insight, whereas most BDD patients retain some insight.
exp: Body dysmorphic disorder (grouped with OCD-related disorders in DSM-5) involves preoccupation with a perceived appearance defect that is minimal or absent on exam, plus repetitive checking/camouflaging behaviours and significant impairment; first-line treatment is SSRIs plus CBT, not cosmetic intervention, and patients should be screened before any cosmetic referral.
